journal_name: ACM Transactions on Interactive Intelligent Systems

abstracts.abstract: The proliferation of human-AI interaction necessitates fundamental rethinking of how users form mental models during engagement with adaptive systems. This paper introduces the Cognitive Dynamics Framework (CDF), a novel theoretical construct that reconceptualizes user understanding as a continuously evolving process rather than a static cognitive state. Grounded in distributed cognition theory and situated learning principles, CDF posits that user mental models undergo three distinct phase transitions: initialization, calibration, and stabilization, each characterized by specific information processing patterns and interaction behaviors. Through longitudinal user studies (N=156) conducted across three distinct interactive intelligent systems—conversational agents, recommender systems, and adaptive learning platforms—we validate CDF's predictive power for user satisfaction and system effectiveness. Our findings reveal that phase transition timing significantly mediates the relationship between system complexity and user trust, challenging prevailing assumptions in user modeling literature. The framework yields three testable predictions that current theories fail to account for: (1) optimal intervention timing varies systematically across cognitive phases, (2) explanation complexity should adapt to user's current phase, and (3) user retention patterns follow phase-dependent trajectories. This paradigm-shifting framework fundamentally transforms how researchers conceptualize human-centered AI evaluation, moving beyond static usability metrics toward dynamic cognitive assessments.

Contemporary recommender systems face a fundamental tension between prediction accuracy and explainability, with existing utility functions treating these objectives as competing priorities. This paper advances a unified preference theory that reconciles this dichotomy by introducing the Constructive Preference Model (CPM), which distinguishes between stated preferences (explicit feedback) and constructive preferences (emerging from interaction patterns). We theoretically derive that user satisfaction in interactive intelligent systems arises from the alignment between system's internal representation and user's evolving constructive preference structure, not merely prediction accuracy. CPM formalizes this relationship through a novel utility function that jointly optimizes representation alignment and explanation quality, parameterized by user expertise level and task complexity. Analytical derivations establish that CPM subsumes existing approaches (matrix factorization, deep collaborative filtering) as special cases under specific parameter constraints, enabling theoretical comparisons. Simulations across three benchmark datasets (MovieLens, Last.fm, Amazon Reviews) demonstrate that CPM achieves statistically significant improvements in recommendation quality (12-18% gain in NDCG) while simultaneously enhancing explanation comprehensibility (p<0.001). Importantly, the model provides theoretical guarantees on the trade-off between exploration and exploitation that adapt to individual user characteristics, offering principled guidance for personalization strategies in recommender systems.

This paper presents MetaMorph, a revolutionary conversational agent architecture that fundamentally reimagines human-AI dialogue through embodied metacognitive mechanisms. Unlike existing conversational agents that process utterances in isolation, MetaMorph maintains a dynamic self-model that continuously reflects on conversation state, interaction history, and user cognitive load. The system comprises three integrated components: (1) a Metacognitive Monitor that tracks conversational coherence and user engagement in real-time, (2) a Strategy Selector that adapts communication strategies based on emerging metacognitive assessments, and (3) an Explanation Generator that produces contextually appropriate justifications aligned with detected user mental models. We deployed MetaMorph across three domains (healthcare consultation, technical support, educational tutoring) with 342 participants in a controlled user study. Results demonstrate that MetaMorph achieves a 34% reduction in misunderstanding instances and 28% improvement in task completion rates compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Crucially, user trust ratings increased significantly (p<0.001), and the system exhibited unprecedented capability to detect and recover from conversational breakdowns. This work introduces a new paradigm for intelligent user interfaces where conversational agents possess metacognitive awareness, fundamentally expanding the design space for human-centered AI systems.

Existing intelligent tutoring systems suffer from a critical limitation: they adapt instruction based on performance metrics but neglect the affective dimensions of learning, leading to suboptimal engagement and knowledge retention. This paper presents AffectiveLearn, a novel system architecture that integrates real-time multimodal affect recognition with adaptive scaffolding strategies in intelligent tutoring systems. AffectiveLearn processes facial expressions, vocal prosody, and interaction behavioral signals through a hierarchical fusion network to construct fine-grained affective state representations across eight emotional dimensions. These representations inform a Reinforcement Learning-based scaffolding engine that dynamically adjusts pedagogical interventions—varying explanation depth, pacing, example selection, and motivational feedback—to optimize both cognitive and emotional learning outcomes. We conducted a 12-week deployment study with 218 students across two high school mathematics courses, comparing AffectiveLearn against an affect-agnostic adaptive system and a non-adaptive control condition. Students using AffectiveLearn demonstrated significantly higher knowledge retention (ES=0.67) and course completion rates (91% vs. 73%) while reporting enhanced learning experience scores. The system successfully identifies learning frustration 3.2 minutes before performance degradation occurs, enabling proactive intervention. AffectiveLearn represents a substantial advancement in personalized learning technology, demonstrating that integrating affect recognition meaningfully improves educational outcomes in interactive learning environments.
